title: Version history
generatedNote: Hand-curated. Big user-facing milestones, grouped by who helped build them.

versions.name: Party 2.0
versions.summary: A crowd on a canvas, and a party that walks out into it.
changes: Party 2.0 (party.webp) sits under Toys: an old-fashioned frame around a modern one, with a drifting crowd on a canvas that reaches for your pointer and a row of buttons above it — Palette, Motion, Readout and Frame — that each open a small tool window you can drag anywhere on the desktop, floating above the window that opened it

Party 2.0's Frame tool bends the window it sits in — turn Warp up and the whole frame goes soft and pulls out of true, title bar, borders and all, with its corners rounding off as it goes; Straighten up puts it back

Party 2.0's canvas is a crowd rather than a scattering of dots: every point is one of a set of little painted figures, walking about in whatever colour the palette is set to — and the Palette tool can swap the whole crowd for rats, for mice, or back to plain dots

Anyone in that crowd can be picked out of it: click a figure on Party 2.0's canvas and a dashed ring marks it, after which the Palette's colour and shape dress that one alone — one rat among the walkers, or a single point left as a dot — with Reset putting it back in step, and a click on empty canvas handing the Palette back to everybody

The old Party (dnd.exe) has moved inside: the roster and the character sheet are one more of Party 2.0's floating tools, and everyone you Save walks out onto the canvas to drift with the crowd under their own name — click one out there and their sheet comes up, and when the party's ten minutes are up they set off across the desktop from wherever they were standing

A character is a person now rather than an empty suit of armour: each one is one of the little painted figures from Party 2.0's crowd, wearing their own gear and bare at the head, hands or feet where they carry none — and since it is the same figure, it takes its colour from the Palette like everybody else. Alignment is a glow behind them instead of patterned wallpaper: its hue tells good from evil, and its shape tells lawful from chaotic, from a tight steady halo to a wide, frayed one

Party 2.0's Frame tool can light the window up as well as bend it: Colour puts the frame and its title bar into the spectrum at once, and Cycle, Pulse and Strobe set it walking round the colours, breathing in and out, and flashing — Lights out puts it back. The strobe will not go past three flashes a second however far you push it, and anyone whose machine is set to prefer less movement gets the colour holding still instead

The Frame tool can also hand Party 2.0's own tool windows the desktop's frame: switch Tool windows from Modern to Framed and the Palette, Motion, Readout, Frame and Party panels each come up in a Windows 95 border and title bar, while the sliders, swatches and readouts inside them stay exactly as modern as they were. A panel wearing the frame does whatever the frame does — it lights up on the same beat and warps out of true along with it

Party 2.0 remembers where you put its tool windows: drag the Palette, or any of the others, somewhere that suits you and closing it and opening it again brings it back to that spot rather than to the edge it started at. Each panel is remembered separately, and one you have never moved still opens in its own slot

Media (player.exe) sits under Tools: open a song or a video — or a whole folder, and it plays everything in it in order — with play, pause, skip, shuffle, repeat, volume and a playlist you can double-click through, and trim with the Delete key or a right-click. Drag along the seek bar and a tooltip shows where you'll land before you let go. Songs get a little green screen under their name that moves with the sound, like an old monitor with scanlines and a glow that trails behind — a View menu swaps it between bars, the waveform itself, and a spectrum scrolling slowly past. It plays old .au sound files too, and starts out with a drone loop queued up. Files can be dropped straight onto it, and they never leave your computer

The media player's previous, stop and next buttons are drawn the same way as play, pause and the rest of the row — square-edged pixel shapes instead of three characters borrowed from the system font, which never quite matched

Projects lists card-binder, the card scanner that fills Collections' card shelf: photograph a trading card — or a whole binder page — and it works out which print it is, prices it, and files it in a binder you can sort and export. It's closed source, so instead of sending you to a repository the entry says so and opens a screenshot of the thing itself

Collections' cards behave like things on a desk: drag one and it stays on top of the pile instead of dropping back underneath the moment you touch another, and picking one up moves it rather than peeling it off the screen as a picture to drop somewhere else

Party 2.0's Motion tool has gained a Trails slider: turn it up and the canvas stops wiping itself clean every frame, so the crowd and the lines strung between them smear across it like a long exposure — Wipe clean takes it back to bare surface without interrupting the drift

Everybody in Party 2.0's crowd has a head again: a handful of the little painted figures were drawn with their heads a shade clear of the shoulders, and had been coming off the paint sheet decapitated

Party 2.0's crowd is twice the crowd it was: a second sheet of the little painted figures has been cut up and added to the first, so there are 163 of them walking about instead of 76 — fewer twins in a canvas full of people

Party 2.0's crowd can be pushed around now: a new Forces tool gives them gravity — with a dial you point wherever you like, not only down — a wind that comes in gusts rather than leaning on them steadily, and a jitter that sets everyone fidgeting. The pointer stops being something they merely draw lines at: set it to attract, repel or orbit and it gathers the crowd in, shoves it away, or swings it round in a circle. And three flocking sliders — separation, alignment and cohesion — turn the drift into a flock that clumps together, falls into step and keeps out of its own way. Let them be hands the canvas back to the old aimless wander

The lines strung between Party 2.0's figures have controls of their own at last: a Links tool sets how strong and how thick they are, how many any one figure is allowed to hold, and whether they run straight or bow out into curves. They can be drawn in ink, in the palette's colour, or in the colours of the two figures at either end so that each line fades from one to the other — and turn Mesh up and the triangles between any three figures standing close together fill in, so the crowd drags a sheet of shattered glass about with it

Party 2.0 keeps a log of itself: the Console tool is a teletype of what the window has been up to — who joined the party, that the density went from 46 to 88, when the party departed — each line stamped with the time it happened and the whole thing scrolling along as it fills. Drag a slider about and it writes down where you started and where you let go, on one line, rather than every step in between

Party 2.0's crowd can be told to stop drifting and arrange: the new Formation tool walks them into a grid, a ring or a spiral — and there is a text field, so they will walk into the shape of whatever you type and stand there spelling it. How tightly they hold the shape is a slider, and so is how restless they are: turn that up and they keep breaking out of it and wandering back into it. The word is sized to the crowd rather than to the window, so turning Density up makes it bigger rather than more crowded

Party 2.0's crowd can be let out: the Frame tool — which already bends and lights the window from inside it — now has a switch that opens the frame altogether, and the crowd wanders off across the desktop, in behind whatever else you have open, with the lines still strung between the ones out there and the ones still inside. Shut it again and they file back in

There is something to roll at last: Party 2.0's Dice tool throws a d20, a d6 or a d100 across the canvas — with advantage or disadvantage, which throws two and shows you which one it kept — and the die tumbles through the crowd, knocks people out of its way and comes to rest showing its number, which is also when the panel tells you what you got. Every roll goes in a log. Roll for initiative and the whole party rolls, takes its number over its head, and lines up across the canvas in order

Party 2.0's Encounters tool gives the party something to do with its ten minutes: roll and something walks in off the edge — a goblin, an owlbear, a dragon — with a reason for being there and a pile of loot for afterwards. The party converges on it and stops just short; everybody else clears the ground around it and drifts back once it has gone. It cannot be fought and there is nothing to win: it is a prompt, the way the roster is a character sheet rather than a character

versions.name: Save & read
versions.summary: Work that sticks around, and a history you can read.
changes: Notepad and Paint remember what you left in them — closing the window, refreshing or shutting down no longer wipes the page — and both have a File menu to start fresh, open a file from your computer, or save your work as a download
This window is easier to read: every change gets its own bullet with room around it, each version shows its name, and older versions fold down to one line — click one to open it

Past searches under the search bar are tidier — each one starts with just how long ago it was made — and clicking one takes you to the issue it became, opened to the right comment, or into Notepad if it never became one — and if that window is already open it stays where it is, with the search added to the page or the issue opened alongside what you had open
Past searches that shouldn't be on show can be taken out of the search box's history, and they stay out after every update

Projects lists midi-scope, a live MIDI analyser with a 3D spectrogram you fly through — it's closed source, so instead of sending you to a repository the entry says so and opens a screenshot of the thing itself
Party (dnd.exe) no longer throws away a half-finished sheet when you click another character — your edits wait for you, marked with a *, until you come back and Save
Moving or resizing a window works the old way now — a dotted outline follows your pointer and the window jumps there when you let go, and Escape leaves it where it was

Collections now opens on a Cards tab holding the Pokémon card collection — each card shows its number, its set and how rare it is — and the cards scatter across the desktop like the albums and paintings do
Maximizing Collections now shows whatever you have picked as big as the window will allow, rather than a stamp in the middle of it

versions.name: Drag & play
versions.summary: Windows that move, faders that play.
changes: Windows can be moved now — grab a title bar and drag it anywhere on the desktop; the window keeps whatever size you gave it
midi.exe's Mod fader and stick finally do something: Mod adds vibrato, and the stick sweeps the filter — left and right for brighter or darker, up and down for more or less resonance
midi.exe's drum pads hit harder — the whole kit is louder next to the keys

midi.exe fits a phone now — the keys stay at the bottom with room for a fingertip, and the pads, knobs, wheels, log and scope take turns in one space above them, with a tall Bank pad beside the drum pads
midi.exe's meters and scope moved into a new View menu, and on a wide window they sit to the right of the knobs instead of pushing the keys down

versions.name: Scope & small screens
versions.summary: See the sound, fit the screen.
changes: midi.exe has a Scope button now: it draws the shape of the sound you're playing above a little 3D spectrogram — the last few seconds of its frequencies stacked back into the distance — and reads out the frequency in Hz, the note it's nearest to and how many cents sharp or flat, plus what's being held and how loud it is

midi.exe folds itself up when the window is narrow — a phone, or a window you've dragged small: the bend, pad and knob sections go behind tabs, the function buttons split into two rows, and the keybed shows as many octaves as will fit at a size you can actually hit, with arrows to move along it
Windows no longer open wider than the screen they're on, so on a phone the title bar and its buttons are where you can reach them
Dropped midi.exe's Edit menu — the Prog button on the panel already steps through the waveforms

versions.name: Party & Projects
versions.summary: A pocket D&D party, and real projects.
changes: Added Party (dnd.exe) under Toys: roll up a D&D character — name, race, class, alignment, level and 4d6-drop-lowest ability scores — and Save it to a party roster that's remembered in your browser. Each one gets a chunky pixel loadout tile laid out like an armour stand — head, chest, hands, legs, feet and what they carry — where class picks the gear, race picks its colours and how tall they stand, and alignment picks the backdrop. A party only stays ten minutes — then it walks out from behind the window and off the desktop, and the roster starts fresh
Projects (projects.txt) now lists real open-source work, starting with cairn, a local-first markdown notes editor. The nine interface demos moved to their own Demos window (demos.txt) under Documents
Each project in projects.txt now shows the description and preview image straight from its GitHub repo, falling back to a hand-written blurb and thumbnail when the repo has none
Added this site itself to projects.txt
about.txt now credits Claude with even more help, not just cleanup work

versions.name: MPK mini
changes: midi.exe is now laid out like an AKAI MPK mini PLUS — pitch bend and mod faders, a thumbstick, eight pads and eight knobs, all of which play and show up in the message log
midi.exe's thumbstick now sends its own two controls instead of doubling up on the bend and mod faders, so you can move all four at once
midi.exe's pads now have two banks — hit Bank to swap between them, and anything still sounding stops on the way out
The labels on midi.exe's front panel sit inside their own frames now, instead of spilling over the box next door
midi.exe's pads now play an actual drum kit — kick, snare, hats, claps, toms and cymbals across two banks, with each pad's piece written on it
midi.exe's eight knobs now do something: filter cutoff and resonance, attack and release, drum tune and decay, echo and volume — with a readout on the display of what you just changed

versions.name: Search & windows
versions.summary: Notes that nudge, windows that resize.
changes: The search-bar scratchpad now nudges me when you finish jotting a thought, so notes don't sit unread
Windows have a working resize grip in the bottom-right corner now — drag it to size a window, and it stays put where you left it
Split the version history into minor releases, so each card here is a short, readable list instead of one long dump

versions.name: Desktop shell
versions.summary: Start menu, Paint, and a tidier desktop.
changes: Renamed the REPL program to Sounds in the Start menu
Swapped the LinkedIn social link for Bluesky
Tidied the Start menu's Programs list into App, Tools, and Toys groups, with Welcome left on its own
Kept the Start menu's submenus on screen in narrow browser windows — one that would run off the right edge now opens to the left instead
Stopped the Issues window from wrapping long lines — they run on and scroll sideways now, like Notepad with word wrap off
Added Paint: a blank white sheet you scribble on with a pencil — pick a colour, change the brush size, and Clear to start over
Made Shut Down / restart fetch the newest published build instead of a cached copy, and stamped the current version on the shutdown and startup screens

versions.name: Collections & Projects
changes: Projects now shows nine interface demos — marked as demos, not client work — with the full set at /mockups/
Gave Collections its own Albums, Paintings, and Songs tabs, with paintings and songs drawn from picked Bluesky posts
Switched the Collections category picker from tabs to toggle buttons that match the Sounds and Keys toolbars

Reworked Collections: the picture tiles now scatter across the whole desktop, you can drag them anywhere and they stay put, and picking one no longer reshuffles the others — the window just grew a little so the selected picture sits centred

versions.name: Keys
versions.summary: A MIDI monitor grows into a synth.
changes: Added the Keys program: lists connected MIDI inputs and logs their messages live
Expanded the Keys monitor with activity meters, a one-octave keyboard, raw message bytes, and a Scan button to grant MIDI access
Keys makes sound now — a built-in synth plays incoming notes and an on-screen keyboard you click, tap, or play with your computer keys, with a square/saw/triangle/sine waveform picker
Keys keeps a running message list you can Play back through the synth, Save as a .mid file, or export as CSV or JSON
Open a .mid file in Keys to load its notes into the message list, then hit Play to hear it
Keys now opens on any browser — no MIDI hardware or Web MIDI support needed, since the on-screen keyboard and .mid playback work on their own
Tidied Keys for phones — narrower window, a two-octave keyboard you can now slide across with one finger, and octave up/down buttons on the full keyboard when it's maximised on a small screen

versions.name: Claude cleanup
versions.summary: Cleanup and deploy plumbing, no new toys.
changes: Swapped the build-VM deploy for a plain scripts/deploy/ pipeline
Ship a minimal production package.json and track the lockfile
Refresh the issues list from GitHub as a deploy step
Cleared out ESLint errors and dead image assets
Added a Claude credit and tidied the README headings

versions.name: Contact fix

versions.name: Codex build-out

Added the Changes program, driven by a generated changelog
Added the Strudel music window with a live oscilloscope
Added the Albums / Collections carousel window

Put Documents first in the Start menu
Added search playback with relative timing to Issues and Changes

Change when issue comments can expand

Start menu, taskbar, and a working shutdown
